lesson.title: The Collision Theory Playbook: Bringing the Rate Factors Together
lesson.summary: Collision theory explains why temperature, concentration, surface area, and molecular orientation all affect reaction rate: each factor changes how often particles collide, how much energy those collisions carry, or how likely a collision is to be aimed correctly.
lesson.body:
Collision theory gives a single unifying explanation for everything that affects how fast a reaction runs. For a reaction to happen, three things must all be true at once: reactant particles must collide, that collision must carry at least the activation energy required to break existing bonds, and the particles must be oriented correctly relative to each other at the instant of impact. Any factor that increases the frequency of collisions meeting all three conditions increases the observed reaction rate.

Concentration and surface area, covered in the previous chapters, both work by increasing plain collision frequency: more dissolved reactant particles per unit volume, or more exposed particles on a solid's surface, simply means more opportunities for reactant particles to meet in the first place.

Temperature works differently, and its effect is larger than intuition might suggest. As temperature rises, particles move faster on average, so they do collide somewhat more often. But the far more important effect is that a much larger fraction of those collisions now carry enough energy to meet or exceed the activation energy. Because the distribution of particle energies spreads out and shifts upward as temperature rises, even a modest temperature increase of around ten degrees Celsius can double or triple a reaction's rate for many reactions, an effect far too large to be explained by the small increase in collision frequency alone. It is really the shifting energy distribution, not just faster movement, that drives the change.

Orientation matters even when a collision is both frequent and energetic enough. If atom X on one molecule needs to bond to atom Y on another, only a collision where those specific parts of each molecule meet properly will succeed; a collision where the wrong ends of the same two molecules happen to strike each other will simply bounce apart unreacted, no matter how forceful or well timed the impact was. Large, structurally complex molecules tend to have a smaller fraction of their collisions land in a workable orientation than small, simple particles do, which is part of why reactions between bulky organic molecules can be much slower than reactions between small atoms or ions, even under otherwise similar conditions.

Put together, the actual rate of a reaction reflects the combined effect of how often particles collide, what fraction of those collisions carry enough energy, and what fraction are correctly oriented. Concentration and surface area raise collision frequency, temperature raises both collision frequency and the energetic fraction, and orientation sets a ceiling on how many collisions can possibly succeed regardless of energy or frequency. A catalyst, by comparison, works by lowering the activation energy itself, which raises the energetic fraction without needing any change in temperature at all.
